audioScript:
Good morning, Midya. It's Friday, July twenty-fourth, twenty twenty-six. Here's what matters today, and there's a genuinely clean thought-leadership thread running through it if you want to pick it up.

Let's start with AI, because two stories landed today that are really the same idea seen through your two lanes, and together they hand you a POV worth publishing.

The first is from The PIE News, and the headline does a lot of the work: AI in admissions — please don't do it just because you can. The argument is that universities are racing to plug AI into recruitment, application screening, and admissions decisions, and very few of them are pausing to ask the harder question of whether they should, and under what guardrails. The piece frames it as a values moment for higher ed — fairness, transparency, and the risk of automating bias at exactly the point in a student's life where a human judgment call matters most. Now, for you this is close to a gift, because it sits precisely at the intersection of your two signature methodologies. This is AI in higher-ed enrollment meeting the public-institution governance lens. In Canada, an admissions AI isn't just an ethics question — it's a FIPPA question, a data-residency question, and a question of whether student personal information is being processed by a model hosted who-knows-where. My honest advice: this is the day to draft the piece you've been circling. Not a hot take about whether AI belongs in admissions — everyone has that. The differentiated angle is the audit checklist: the ten questions a Canadian institution's registrar and enrollment office should be able to answer before they turn an admissions AI on. Where does the data live? Who reviews the model's decisions? Is there a human override? Can an applicant contest an AI-influenced outcome? That checklist is a product, and this article is the news hook to launch it.

The second AI story comes from HousingWire, and it's the real-estate mirror image of the same truth. The headline is: AI makes anyone visible, authority is the new scarcity. The core finding is that generative AI is flooding housing and mortgage feeds with near-identical content — everyone's using the same tools to produce the same competent, forgettable posts — so visibility itself has been commoditized. And here's the number that should stick with you: trust in AI for home search is down to sixteen percent, and fifty-five percent of people still want a human when it comes to the mortgage. So the value has migrated. It's no longer about being seen; it's about being believed. Authority — a genuine point of view, a defensible position, actual proof — is what's now scarce. Midya, this is your AI Search Readiness thesis stated in a real estate accent. When you tell a brokerage that showing up in AI Overviews and ChatGPT isn't the finish line, this is the evidence. The finish line is being the source the AI trusts and the human still wants to call. If you want a second piece of content this week, the pairing is powerful: authority is the scarce asset in both enrollment and real estate, and generative search rewards the brands that have built it. Two industries, one thesis — that's exactly the cross-lane positioning that makes you look like a category thinker rather than a vendor.

Now to the organizations worth tracking closely.

Capilano University is in the news for hosting Whistler Film Festival talent development programs, with the framing of amplifying Canadian voices. On its face it's a cultural-partnership story, but read it as a brand play. A mid-sized institution is anchoring its identity to Canada's creative industries and to a marquee regional event — that's differentiation strategy in a crowded BC market where nearly every school is fighting for the same domestic applicants as the international pipeline tightens. Worth watching whether they build a recruitment narrative around it or let it stay a nice press release.

Also on the radar: AACRAO's annual conference produced coverage of a University of Phoenix vice provost presenting on credit transfer and learner mobility. The University of Phoenix specifics matter less than the signal about where the registrar and admissions community is putting its attention — transfer pathways and learner mobility are the plumbing of enrollment, and they're increasingly where AI and process modernization collide. If the people who run admissions operations are gathering around mobility, that's a preview of the problems your higher-ed prospects will be trying to solve next.

Staying in higher ed, the international-student policy story keeps developing, and today brings an update to what we covered earlier this week.

The Economic Times reports that Canada's new guidance spells out the stricter study-permit and post-graduate work-permit requirements in more concrete terms. This is the compliance clarification we flagged Wednesday, now with sharper detail on what applicants and institutions actually have to demonstrate. The strategic read hasn't changed but it's intensifying: the international enrollment funnel that so many Canadian institutions leaned on for a decade is becoming a compliance-and-conversion problem, not a volume game. Every additional documentation requirement is another point where qualified students fall out of the pipeline — and remember, an earlier report this week found nearly half of Canadian study-visa refusals were deemed preventable, often down to paperwork rather than money. For anyone advising on enrollment marketing, that's the opening: the value isn't just filling the top of the funnel anymore, it's protecting conversion through a funnel that's now booby-trapped with compliance friction. Institutions that treat applicant support and documentation clarity as a marketing function — not just a back-office function — will hold their numbers while others bleed out.

One more from the Canadian higher-ed file, and it's a reputational-risk case study. University Affairs reports that the University of Alberta's Campus Saint-Jean is wrestling with the legacy of its founders — figures who represent French-Canadian survival to some and colonial oppression to others. Decolonization efforts have collided with Franco-Albertan heritage, and there's no clean resolution. I flag it not for the politics but for the brand lesson: this is what institutional identity risk looks like when history, community stakeholders, and modern values pull in three directions at once. Every institution carries some version of this, and how leadership communicates through it — with candour versus defensiveness — becomes part of the brand. It's a useful reference point when a client asks how to handle a heritage or naming controversy of their own.

On the marketing and business front, two items worth your attention.

At the agency level, Brandon Cooke has joined BarkleyOKRP to drive what they're calling thoughtful growth, succeeding longtime CMO Jason Parks. The word thoughtful is doing quiet work there — it's code for measured, margin-conscious expansion rather than growth at any cost. Combined with the M&A report we discussed earlier this week showing more than half of independent agency owners want to sell, you can see the shape of the market: independents consolidating, senior talent reshuffling, and a general repricing of what growth should feel like. For a solo consulting practice, that's actually opportunity — the mid-market clients those shifting agencies serve are exactly the ones who value a nimble, senior advisor over a big-box retainer.

And a brand case study I liked: Adweek on legendary toy brands finding a new customer in adults. Heritage toy makers are deliberately marketing to nostalgic grown-ups, extending their demographic through emotional positioning rather than reinventing the product. It's a clean example of brand elasticity — you don't always need a new thing, sometimes you need a new audience for the thing you already own. That's a framing that translates directly to a university selling continuing education to alumni, or a brokerage repositioning for a different buyer cohort.

Turning to real estate and the industry's operating environment, two HousingWire pieces sharpen how the business is changing.

The first: modernization delays are becoming competitive liabilities. Lenders and servicers report that legacy systems are throttling efficiency and quietly raising compliance and security exposure, and while most are attempting migrations, long timelines leave them stuck mid-transition. The takeaway that matters for a brokerage audience is that technology debt is no longer a back-office inconvenience — it's a front-line competitive disadvantage and a risk-management problem. When you talk to real estate operators about AI and agent productivity, this is the sober counterweight: the shiny new tools don't work if the underlying systems are held together with tape.

The second is a data-literacy reframe that's genuinely useful. HousingWire argues the homeownership rate isn't what you think. The famous sixty-five percent figure is actually an owner-occupancy rate — it counts owner-occupied units, not adult owners. A proposed homeowners-to-population ratio suggests only about fifty-three percent of US adults actually own a home. It's American data, but the principle travels: the headline metric everyone quotes about housing may be systematically overstating how many people are actually in the market. For anyone building affordability narratives or investment theses, it's a reminder to check what the number is really measuring before you build a story on it.

Closer to home now, in Sun Peaks and Kamloops.

The good news first: Sun Peaks is reporting indicators of a strong summer, with bikers and racers rolling into the community for the mountain-bike season and race events. Robust summer visitation is a healthy sign for the resort economy and, by extension, for short-term-rental demand in the village — worth keeping in the back of your mind on the property side.

In Kamloops, CMHA is opening a fifty-five-bed facility on McGill to house people transitioning out of shelters toward permanent homes. It's part of the city's ongoing supportive-housing buildout — a meaningful piece of the local housing-and-services picture, and one that connects to the broader affordability and homelessness conversations that keep surfacing in council coverage.

A quick look at the wider world, chosen for relevance rather than noise.

Canada and Ecuador are signing a free trade agreement in Ottawa today. On its own it's a modest deal, but it fits the pattern of Ottawa actively diversifying trade relationships in a world where the old reliable partnerships feel less reliable. Watch this space — trade diversification is quietly becoming a defining theme of Canadian economic policy.

And a framing piece from Axios that I think is worth internalizing: it's one choke point after another in the global economy. The phrase choke point is having a moment because the same word now describes the bottlenecks straining oil markets, the AI buildout, and shipping lanes all at once — from the Strait of Hormuz to the Red Sea. The deeper point is that the old, frictionless global order is giving way to one defined by bottlenecks, competition, and outright conflict. For a senior operator, that's the macro weather system behind everything else — supply fragility is now a permanent planning assumption, not a crisis to wait out.

Two health items today, both from sources that clear the bar.

From Nature Medicine, the LITMUS prospective study on fatty liver disease. The finding: blood-based serum biomarkers outperformed imaging for identifying patients at risk of steatohepatitis — that's MASH — while elastography was better for staging advanced fibrosis and cirrhosis. In plain terms, we're getting closer to reliable, non-invasive ways to catch metabolic liver disease early, without a biopsy. Given how tightly liver health tracks with the broader cardiometabolic picture, it's a meaningful step for screening.

And from STAT News, a US Senate committee has advanced a bipartisan bill targeting ultra-processed foods with front-of-package warning labels and restrictions on junk-food advertising. Set aside the politics — the signal is that nutrition policy is shifting toward front-of-package intervention, and unusual bipartisan alliances formed around it. If warning labels on ultra-processed foods become normalized in the US, that framework tends to migrate northward eventually. Worth tracking as a slow-moving change to the food environment your family lives in.

Finally, the family-safety item. BC wildfires are prompting fresh evacuations as hot, dry conditions persist across the province. There's a specific development on the transportation side: Highway 3 has reopened after the Anderson Creek fire threat eased, but the Trans-Canada remains closed near Boston Bar in the Fraser Canyon. If anyone in your circle is moving between the Interior and the coast this weekend, that closure is the one to plan around, and conditions are shifting daily — check before anyone drives.

That's your Friday, Midya. If you do one thing with this briefing, let it be the AI thread — the admissions piece and the authority-versus-visibility piece are the same argument in two markets you sell into, and stitching them together into a single POV is exactly the kind of category-level thinking that builds the thought-leadership reputation you're aiming for by next year. Everything else you can skim; that one you can build on. Have a focused weekend, and keep an eye on those fire updates before anyone hits the highway.
